bibliography.corrections: give the page range: 115(2): 234–238 (April 1986). The contents list places Blumer's article at p. 234 and the next article (Licht) at p. 239; Crossref gives only the first page. Animal Diversity Web also lists 115: 234–238
bibliography.note: Blumer, L. S. 1986. The function of parental care in the brown bullhead Ictalurus nebulosus. American Midland Naturalist 115(2): 234–238, doi:10.2307/2425859. It is a full article, not a note. In Blumer's own reference list in the 1986 Behav. Ecol. Sociobiol. paper it is 'Blumer LS (1986) … Am Midl Nat (in press)', unlettered; there his Am. Midl. Nat. natural-history paper is '1985a' and the EBF paper '1985b'.

claims.claim: broods whose parents were both removed "never reached the larval stage" (Blumer 1986a, abstract; quoted)
claims.note: Full text not read. The ABSTRACT'S WORDS ARE DIFFERENT: 'When both attending adults were experimentally removed from their egg mass, broods always failed to reach the larval stage of development.' The paper's quotation marks enclose words that are not in the abstract: quote it exactly. The abstract also says most of these egg masses disappeared soon after the parents were removed (predation), and that with predation absent or predators excluded 'all embryos still failed to survive to the larval stage', which it puts down to fungal infection and insufficient gas exchange.

claims.paper: §3.6.2; Table 3.6-1 (brown bullhead, care); Table 3.5-2 (brown bullhead, spawning)
claims.claim: broods attended by both parents in 56.2 % of cases and by the male alone in 39.3 % (paper cites 'Blumer 1985, 1986b, via Animal Diversity Web')
claims.note: ATTRIBUTION. Animal Diversity Web (Blumer_1985_viaADW.txt, lines 424–426) says 'Blumer (1985 and 1986a) found males to be primary caregivers: 56.2% … both sexes, 39.3% by males only, and 4.5% by females only. Maximum length of parental care is 29 days.' ADW's reference list holds three Blumer works, unlettered: Behav. Ecol. Sociobiol. 19: 97–104 (1986); Am. Midl. Nat. 1985: 318–330 ('Reproductive natural history…'); Am. Midl. Nat. 115: 234–238 (1986, this paper). So ADW's '1986a' could be either 1986 paper; the paper's own lettering makes this one 1986a. Neither this abstract nor the 1985 Am. Midl. Nat. abstract nor the EBF and BES abstracts (read by other readers) prints 56.2/39.3/4.5 %. Which Blumer full text holds the split is not established. Until one is read, cite 'Animal Diversity Web (Guth 2011), citing Blumer 1985 and 1986a', with ADW's 1985 being the Am. Midl. Nat. 114(2): 318–330 paper.

claims.claim: parental care up to 29 d (Blumer 1985, via ADW)
claims.note: ADW gives the 29-day maximum in the same sentence group it credits to 'Blumer (1985 and 1986a)'. CONFLICT: the abstract of Blumer 1985, Am. Midl. Nat. 114: 318–330 (OpenAlex, saved as Blumer_1986a.openalex-abstract-of-Blumer1985-AmMidlNat.txt) says adults care for eggs, larvae and juveniles 'as long as 20 days after oviposition'. This 1986a abstract gives no duration. Flag 29 d as unverified and possibly wrong; the primary abstract says 20 d.

notes: WHICH BLUMER WORK HOLDS WHICH VALUE (from what could be read): (1) Blumer 1985, 'Reproductive natural history of the brown bullhead Ictalurus nebulosus in Michigan', Am. Midl. Nat. 114(2): 318–330, doi:10.2307/2425607 — abstract (OpenAlex): spawning late May and early June at Munro Lake, Michigan; 'Most oviposition occurs during a 10- to 15-day period each year'; care up to 20 days after oviposition; one mate per season; males alone care more often than females alone; males the principal care-givers. This is the source of src/w3/fish3.js:707's '10–15-day window' and of the late May–June timing; it is NOT the EBF paper that the paper's references call 'Blumer 1985'. ADW's other 'Blumer (1985)' numbers (spawning most often in the first 16 days of June over a four-year study; hatching at a mean of 5.6 d, up to 13 d; larval stage mean 4.4 d, 4–9 d) are credited by ADW to 1985 alone, and ADW's only 1985 reference is this Am. Midl. Nat. paper. (2) Blumer 1985, EBF 12(3): 231–236 — abstract (Blumer_1985 evidence): most broods attended by both sexes; two care-givers better than one; no percentages. (3) This paper, 1986a — abstract: removal experiment; predation, fungus and gas exchange; minnows and sunfishes the most frequent nest intruders; few broods survive to the normal end of care; most mortality early; no percentages or durations. (4) Blumer 1986b, Behav. Ecol. Sociobiol. 19(2): 97–104 — abstract (Blumer_1986b evidence): sex roles in care; no percentages. The lead's description is slightly off: ADW credits the June spawning window to Blumer (1985) alone, not to '1985 and 1986a'; only the 56.2/39.3/4.5 % split (and, in the same paragraph, the 29-day maximum) is credited to '1985 and 1986a'. Fetch list for the human: JSTOR 2425607 (1985) and 2425859 (1986a), and Springer BF00299944 (1986b): the split is most likely in 1985 Am. Midl. Nat. or 1986b, but that is a guess.
